title: Alcohol consumption and cardiovascular disease: A Mendelian randomization study

claims.statement: In Chinese men and in people of European descent, genetically higher alcohol intake compared with genetically lower intake is associated with higher blood pressure and with more high blood pressure (hypertension), and in the Chinese study the rise for each gram was about the same as with self-reported drinking; no paper read gives the absolute risk of hypertension by amount drunk. In 161,498 genotyped Chinese adults, men's systolic blood pressure was 4.3 mm Hg higher (95% CI 3.7 to 4.9) per 280 g of ethanol a week (40 g a day) of genotype-predicted mean intake, which, if the rise is even, is about 1.5 mm Hg per 100 g a week (editors' calculation), against 4.8 mm Hg (4.5 to 5.1) per 280 g a week of self-reported usual intake among men who drank; in women, few of whom drink, the same genotypes went with 0.6 mm Hg lower pressure (−1.0 to −0.1) (Millwood et al., 2019). In 56 European-descent studies, carriers of the ADH1B variant, who reported 17% less drinking, had systolic pressure 0.88 mm Hg lower (0.56 to 1.19 lower) and odds of hypertension of 0.94 (0.91 to 0.98; 104,570 people with hypertension), but the lower pressure was as large in people who said they did not drink (0.80 mm Hg lower) as in people who drank lightly to moderately (0.68 lower), which points either to misreported drinking or to a path other than current drinking (Holmes et al., 2014). In UK Biobank, a genetic score for alcohol use disorder was associated with hypertension, odds ratio 1.28 (1.18 to 1.39) per standard deviation of genetically predicted intake (Biddinger et al., 2022), and in European summary data genetically predicted drinking went with higher systolic and diastolic pressure, in units the paper's figure does not make clear (Larsson et al., 2020). In UK Biobank's self-reported data, the lower hypertension risk of people who drank moderately, against people who did not drink, was no longer statistically clear once six lifestyle factors were allowed for. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Millwood et al. 2019 (men; per 280 g/week, which is 40 g/day): systolic blood pressure +4.3 mm Hg (3.7–4.9) genetic, +4.8 (4.5–5.1) conventional among current drinkers; about +1.5 mm Hg per 100 g/week if linear (editors' calculation); women −0.6 (−1.0 to −0.1). Holmes et al. 2014 (intake-lowering ADH1B variant; 17.2% fewer units a week): systolic −0.88 mm Hg (−1.19 to −0.56), hypertension OR 0.94 (0.91–0.98); by self-reported drinking −0.80 (none), −0.68 (more than 0 to under 21 units/week), −1.70 (21 or more). Biddinger et al. 2022 (OR per SD of genetically predicted intake): hypertension 1.28 (1.18–1.39); within categories per 1 drink/day of allele score 1.3 (light), 1.7 (moderate), 2.6 (highest); conventional moderate-intake difference not significant after six lifestyle factors. Larsson et al. 2020: systolic 0.12 (0.05–0.20) and diastolic 0.15 (0.05–0.25) per SD of log drinks/week, units unclear. No absolute risks of hypertension by intake.

claims.statement: In people of European descent and in Chinese men, genetic variants that predict more drinking, compared with variants that predict less, are associated with more coronary heart disease in the European studies but not with heart attacks in the Chinese study; in its main analysis none of the four genetic studies read found lower coronary risk with genetically higher intake, none can show the shape of the curve at low intake with confidence, and a published critique argues that such studies remain observational and have biases of their own. No study gives absolute risks. In 56 European-descent studies (261,991 people), carriers of a variant of the alcohol-metabolising gene ADH1B reported 17.2% less drinking (95% CI 15.6% to 18.9%) and had lower odds of coronary heart disease (odds ratio 0.90, 0.84 to 0.96; 20,259 events); the authors had predicted that a protective effect of light to moderate drinking would show as higher odds in carriers who drank lightly to moderately, but the odds were similar at every level of drinking and each of those estimates was compatible with no difference (more than 0 to under 7 UK units of 7.9 g a week, 0.90, 0.79 to 1.02), and the variant went with lower blood pressure even in people who said they did not drink (Holmes et al., 2014). In UK Biobank (371,463 people), a genetic score built from variants for alcohol use disorder was associated with coronary artery disease, odds ratio 1.38 (1.10 to 1.74) per standard deviation of genetically predicted intake (a unit the paper does not define), and curves fitted with a method whose key assumption was not tested rose from the first drink, though a second score suggested no rise below roughly 7 to 14 drinks of 14 g a week, with slight decreases at modest intake for hypertension and in some analyses in women (Biddinger et al., 2022). In European summary data with up to 94 variants, the odds ratio was 1.16 (1.00 to 1.36) per standard deviation of log drinks a week and 1.08 (0.91 to 1.27) after allowing for genetic liability to smoking, which the variants also predicted; the ADH1B variant alone was associated with coronary artery disease (Larsson et al., 2020). In 161,498 genotyped Chinese adults, men's genotype-predicted mean intakes (4 to 256 g a week by group) were not associated with heart attack (relative risk 0.96, 0.78 to 1.18, per 280 g a week, which is 40 g a day; 1,696 cases) or with coronary heart disease (1.05, 0.94 to 1.17), although self-reported drinking in the same men showed lower heart-attack rates at moderate intake than in non-drinkers (Millwood et al., 2019). Three epidemiologists (Mukamal, Stampfer & Rimm, 2020; no funding or interests statement printed) argue that such analyses can be biased by ancestry, by parents' genes and drinking, by weak links between genes and reported intake, by genes that act through acetaldehyde rather than amount, by lowering heavy drinking days together with average intake, and by testing lifelong rather than adult drinking; they quantify none of these and report no figures from the studies they criticize, and Roerecke and Rehm (2014) likewise set the ADH1B result aside because the variant also lowers binge drinking. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Holmes et al. 2014 (56 studies, 261,991 European-descent people; ADH1B rs1229984 A-allele carriers against non-carriers): weekly intake 17.2% lower (15.6% to 18.9%), binge drinking OR 0.78 (0.73–0.84), abstention 1.27 (1.21–1.34); coronary heart disease OR 0.90 (0.84–0.96; 20,259 events; I² 17%), 0.81 (0.72–0.91) in four studies with at least 1,000 events; self-reported non-drinkers 0.98 (0.88–1.10), drinkers 0.86 (0.78–0.94), difference P = 0.095; light (more than 0 to under 7 UK units/week of 7.9 g) 0.90 (0.79–1.02), moderate (7 to under 21) 0.89 (0.75–1.06), heavy (21 or more) 0.97 (0.76–1.24), trend P = 0.83; systolic blood pressure in self-reported non-drinkers −0.80 mm Hg (−1.41 to −0.19); no instrumental-variable estimate. Biddinger et al. 2022 (UK Biobank, 371,463; 5-variant score for alcohol use disorder, F 780; OR per SD of genetically predicted intake): coronary artery disease 1.38 (1.10–1.74; P = .006), myocardial infarction 1.37 (1.05–1.78; P = .02, above the paper's threshold of P < .008); nonlinear: quadratic fit best (P < .001), risk rising from zero intake with the primary score; secondary score: no rise until roughly 7 to 14 drinks (14 g) a week. Larsson et al. 2020 (up to 94 variants; per SD of log drinks/week): coronary artery disease 1.16 (1.00–1.36; P = 0.052), 1.08 (0.91–1.27) adjusted for genetic liability to smoking initiation; never-smokers 1.39 (0.98–1.96); instrument and smoking initiation OR 1.24 (1.15–1.33); ADH1B variant alone, positive (P < 0.05). Millwood et al. 2019 (China Kadoorie Biobank men; six genotype–area groups, mean intake 4 to 256 g/week; per 280 g/week, which is 40 g/day): myocardial infarction RR 0.96 (0.78–1.18; 1,696 cases), coronary heart disease 1.05 (0.94–1.17; 6,145 cases); single variants (GG against AG) myocardial infarction rs671 1.02 (0.92–1.13), rs1229984 1.11 (0.95–1.31); women 0.94 (0.74–1.20). Mukamal et al. 2020: no estimates. No absolute risks in any study.

claims.statement: In Chinese men and in people of European descent, genetically higher alcohol intake compared with genetically lower intake is associated with more stroke, most clearly with bleeding into the brain (intracerebral haemorrhage), and the Chinese study found no sign of a lower risk at low intake; cohort studies comparing people who drink with people who do not found no overall difference in stroke but more strokes at higher intakes. No paper read gives absolute risks of stroke by amount. In 161,498 genotyped Chinese adults from ten areas, followed about 10 years, men's stroke risk rose steadily across six groups whose genotypes and area predicted mean intakes of 4 to 256 g of ethanol a week: per 100 g a week (about 14 g a day, editors' arithmetic) ischaemic stroke 1.09 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.14; 5,709 cases), intracerebral haemorrhage 1.18 (1.12 to 1.24; 2,790 cases) and all stroke 1.12 (1.09 to 1.16); the lowest group, in which two thirds did not drink, showed no sign of a raised risk, and the next two groups (about 100 g a week) had higher, not lower, risk of ischaemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage than the three lowest groups pooled (about 25 g a week); the same genotypes showed no association in women, few of whom drink (ischaemic stroke 0.98, 0.88 to 1.09; intracerebral haemorrhage 0.96, 0.82 to 1.12); and self-reported drinking in the same men showed a U shape, with lower stroke risk at about 100 g a week than in non-drinkers and former drinkers (Millwood et al., 2019). If, and only if, there is no protective effect and the relation is log-linear, those authors estimate that alcohol caused about 8 in 100 ischaemic strokes and 16 in 100 intracerebral haemorrhages among the men studied (a model estimate). In European-descent summary data the odds of stroke were 1.27 (1.12 to 1.45) per standard deviation of genetically predicted log drinks a week, 1.21 (1.05 to 1.40) after allowing for genetic liability to smoking; ischaemic stroke 1.26 (1.09 to 1.46) and intracerebral haemorrhage 3.53 (1.70 to 7.32) (Larsson et al., 2020); in UK Biobank, a genetic score for alcohol use disorder gave 1.26 (1.04 to 1.54), not significant at that paper's threshold for six outcomes (Biddinger et al., 2022). Carriers of the ADH1B variant, who reported 17% less drinking, had lower odds of ischaemic stroke in the studies with subtype data (0.83, 0.72 to 0.95) but no difference in all stroke (0.98, 0.90 to 1.07; 10,164 strokes) (Holmes et al., 2014). In cohort studies, people who drank had, against non-drinkers (most groups including former drinkers), no different risk of new stroke (0.98, 0.91 to 1.06; 17 studies) or of stroke death (1.06, 0.91 to 1.23; 10 studies), and against lifetime abstainers a higher risk of stroke death (1.29, 1.09 to 1.53; 3 studies); by intake, new strokes were less common at up to 14.9 g a day (0.81 and 0.80; 3 studies each) and more common above 60 g a day (1.62, 1.32 to 1.98; 4 studies) (Ronksley et al., 2011); in the GBD 2016 curves ischaemic stroke dipped at low intake without statistical significance. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Millwood et al. 2019 (China Kadoorie Biobank men; genetic, per 280 g/week of genotype-predicted mean intake): ischaemic stroke RR 1.27 (1.13–1.43; 5,709 cases), intracerebral haemorrhage 1.58 (1.36–1.84; 2,790), all stroke 1.38 (1.26–1.51; 9,189); per 100 g/week 1.09 (1.04–1.14), 1.18 (1.12–1.24), 1.12 (1.09–1.16); single variants (GG against AG) stroke 1.19 (1.13–1.24) rs671 and 1.19 (1.11–1.27) rs1229984; women ischaemic stroke 0.98 (0.88–1.09), intracerebral haemorrhage 0.96 (0.82–1.12); conventional, current drinkers per 280 g/week, 1.28 (1.19–1.38), 1.59 (1.37–1.85), 1.35 (1.27–1.44), with a U shape against non-drinkers (not printed); attributable shares if there is no protection and the relation is log-linear: about 8% of ischaemic strokes and 16% of intracerebral haemorrhages in men. Larsson et al. 2020 (per SD of genetically predicted log drinks/week): stroke OR 1.27 (1.12–1.45), adjusted for smoking liability 1.21 (1.05–1.40); ischaemic stroke 1.26 (1.09–1.46); intracerebral haemorrhage 3.53 (1.70–7.32); subarachnoid haemorrhage (UK Biobank) 2.47 (1.08–5.62); ADH1B variant alone ischaemic stroke 1.31 (1.05–1.65), intracerebral haemorrhage 11.5 (1.31–101.46). Biddinger et al. 2022: stroke 1.26 (1.04–1.54; P = .021, threshold P < .008). Holmes et al. 2014 (intake-lowering variant): all stroke 0.98 (0.90–1.07), ischaemic stroke 0.83 (0.72–0.95). Ronksley et al. 2011 (cohorts; against non-drinkers, mostly current): incident stroke 0.98 (0.91–1.06), stroke death 1.06 (0.91–1.23); against lifetime abstainers 0.93 (0.85–1.02) and 1.29 (1.09–1.53); incident stroke by intake (under 2.5 to over 60 g/day) 0.81, 0.80, 0.92, 1.15, 1.62 (1.32–1.98); haemorrhagic 1.14 (0.97–1.34), ischaemic 0.92 (0.85–1.00). No absolute risks in any paper read.

claims.statement: In people of European descent, mostly in UK Biobank, genetically higher alcohol intake compared with genetically lower intake is associated with more peripheral artery disease and possibly with abdominal aortic aneurysm and atrial fibrillation, while results for heart failure differ between the two genetic studies read, and no association was found with blood clots in the veins; the findings come from two studies whose outcome data overlap, some rest on few cases, and no absolute risks are given. Per standard deviation of genetically predicted log drinks a week (a unit the paper does not convert into drinks), the odds ratios were 3.05 (95% CI 1.92 to 4.85) for peripheral artery disease (3,415 cases), 2.55 (1.49 to 4.35) after allowing for genetic liability to smoking; 2.60 (1.15 to 5.89) for abdominal aortic aneurysm (1,094 cases), 2.29 (0.89 to 5.93) after that allowance; 1.17 (1.00 to 1.37) for atrial fibrillation, 1.11 (0.93 to 1.32) after it; 1.00 (0.68 to 1.47) for heart failure; 1.04 (0.77 to 1.39) for venous thromboembolism; and 1.03 (0.56 to 1.90) for narrowing of the aortic valve, for which two other methods suggested a positive association and one indicated pleiotropy (Larsson et al., 2020). With the ADH1B variant alone, genetically higher intake was associated with peripheral artery disease, aortic valve stenosis and abdominal aortic aneurysm. In UK Biobank, a genetic score for alcohol use disorder was associated with atrial fibrillation (1.24, 1.08 to 1.44; 14,367 cases) and heart failure (1.39, 1.08 to 1.78; 5,812 cases), the heart-failure result not significant at that paper's threshold for six outcomes (Biddinger et al., 2022). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
claims.magnitude: Larsson et al. 2020 (OR per SD of genetically predicted log drinks/week; inverse-variance weighted, then adjusted for genetic liability to smoking initiation): peripheral artery disease 3.05 (1.92–4.85), 2.55 (1.49–4.35); abdominal aortic aneurysm 2.60 (1.15–5.89), 2.29 (0.89–5.93); atrial fibrillation 1.17 (1.00–1.37), 1.11 (0.93–1.32); heart failure 1.00 (0.68–1.47), 0.88 (0.57–1.37); venous thromboembolism 1.04 (0.77–1.39), 1.05 (0.75–1.47); aortic valve stenosis 1.03 (0.56–1.90), 0.94 (0.46–1.91), with pleiotropy indicated by MR-Egger; ADH1B variant alone positive (P < 0.05) for peripheral artery disease, aortic valve stenosis and abdominal aortic aneurysm. Biddinger et al. 2022 (OR per SD of genetically predicted consumption): atrial fibrillation 1.24 (1.08–1.44; P = .003), heart failure 1.39 (1.08–1.78; P = .009, threshold P < .008). No absolute risks.
